list.listitem: While historical cases presented with severe respiratory distress, recent H5N1 cases in the U.S. (2024–2025) have been predominantly mild, with conjunctivitis (pink eye) reported in 93% of cases and fever in 49%. Clinicians should suspect H5N1 in patients with conjunctivitis and relevant animal exposure. Confirm diagnosis with real time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) test from nasal aspirate. C
Patients typically present with rapid progression to acute respiratory distress syndrome and are at risk of death. B

First-line treatment is oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days based on uncontrolled case series (oseltamivir 150 mg twice daily for 10 days is an option). Optionally, adding baloxavir 40 to 80 mg once may reduce shedding but has not been shown to reduce mortality or length of hospital stay in a study of severe influenza. B
Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for household contacts (oseltamivir 75 mg/day for 7-10 days after last known exposure). C

background.definition: Avian influenza is an infection caused by a virus found chiefly in birds that can infect humans, with serious consequences that include death.

list.listitem: The first human case of Avian influenza was in Hong Kong 1997; as of March 18, 2008, 373 cases had been reported of which 236 were fatal.
The true incidence is unknown because of underreporting of mild or asymptomatic cases.

However seroprevalance studies suggest that poultry exposes populations have a low seroprevalence for H5N1 antibodies (0.7%-3.2%) suggesting that subclinical and clinically mild infections are not common.
There is risk of a pandemic if the virus mutates to a highly infectious form (highly pathogenic avian influenza) that is easily transmitted from person to person.

An increase in both the variety and prevalence of avian influenza subtypes jumping to humans, with concerning mutations that increase human receptor affinity has been reported. Outbreaks of H5, H7, H9, and emerging subtypes such as H3N8, alongside significant regional and seasonal trends,point to avian influenza's adaptability and the heightened risk for transmission from animals to humans.
If a pandemic occurs, virtually no one will have immunity.
Avian influenza A, specifically the H5N1 subtype.

Transmission to humans is likely through contact with material from infected birds such as respiratory secretions, feces, feathers, organs, and blood, and possibly from contaminated surfaces. Airborne transmission is unlikely but still a concern in clinical settings.

However, a study also found that H5N1 replicates in cattle’s mammary glands, with high viral loads in milk, allowing undetected spread across multiple states, resulting in the first case of mammal-to-human transmission in a dairy worker who developed conjunctivitis after exposure. Cow-to-cow transmission was also observed, although respiratory spread was deemed unlikely.
The majority of recent U.S. cases involved workers with direct exposure to infected dairy cows.
Infection with the influenza A virus (H5N1 subtype) causes diffuse alveolar damage. The rapidly progressing damage may be related to cytokine dysregulation and/or direct viral invasion.
Clinically, infected individuals present with pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, and multi-organ failure.
Register individuals in high-contact activities with animal health/public health authorities. C

Use personal protective equipment (protective clothing, heavy gloves and boots, goggles, masks, with training in its use), frequently wash hands, and learn how to disinfect and/or dispose of potentially contaminated items. The virus is inactivated by soaps, detergents, alcohols, and chlorination. C
Monitor individuals in high-contact activities for fever and influenza-like illness for 7 days after the last day of exposure. C
In settings where personal protective equipment is inadequate, consider starting oseltamivir 75 mg once daily on date of first exposure, to be completed 7 to 10 days after the last exposure. C
Consider seasonal influenza vaccine to minimize other influenza-like illnesses (not intended to protect against H5N1 infection). C
Vaccines specific for avian influenza are under development.
Patients typically present with fever (89%-100%), dyspnea (37%-89%), cough (71%-98%), sore throat (32%-88%), pneumonia (61%-100%), and less commonly vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and myalgias. C
RT-PCR test from nasal aspirate, throat swab, and/or tracheal aspirate is the recommended diagnostic test, but it is only 67% sensitive. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Usually less severe with less rapid progression of illness
Elevated white count, positive sputum smear/cultures

list.listitem: While historical cases presented with severe respiratory distress, recent H5N1 cases in the U.S. (2024–2025) have been predominantly mild, with conjunctivitis (pink eye) reported in 93% of cases and fever in 49%. Clinicians should suspect H5N1 in patients with conjunctivitis and relevant animal exposure.
The incubation period is 7 days or less, often only 2 to 5 days.
In five case series between 2004 and 2005, the following symptoms were present: fever (89%-100%), dyspnea (37%-89%), cough (71%-98%), sore throat (32%-88%), and pneumonia (61%-100%).
Dyspnea and cough were somewhat less common in more recent series. Less common symptoms in these series were vomiting, diarrhea, headache, and myalgias.
Inquire about a history of exposure to poultry, wild birds, or infected humans in countries known to have H5N1.
Physical examination is nonspecific and typical of influenza or pneumonia.
In five case series, leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated aminotransferase levels were commonly seen.
RT-PCR of nasal aspirate and throat swab is the preferred diagnostic test. If possible, tracheal aspirates should also be obtained.

RT-PCR should be done in any patients (in hospital or outpatient) with all of the following: documented temperature of over 38 degrees Celsius, symptoms of sore throat, cough, or shortness of breath, and history of suspicious contact within 10 days of beginning of illness. Suspicious contact refers to that in a country with H5N1, either to domestic birds or poultry, or with a patient known or suspected of having H5N1.

RT-PCR is 67% sensitive and 95% specific (LR+ 6.6, LR− 0.35), so a single negative result does not rule out the diagnosis. If clinical suspicion remains strong, the test should be repeated (obtain throat or tracheal aspirates if possible in addition to nasal).
The current rapid antigen detection assay has low sensitivity and is therefore not preferred. One combined estimate of sensitivity is 17%.
Chest X ray often shows infiltrate.

A study of 121 patients with avian flu and 2603 with other acute RTI in China identified a clinical rule for distinguishing avian influenza. Predictors of avian flu included male sex, poultry exposure, fever, hemoptysis or shortness of breath. Hazy or pneumonia consolidation on CXR and leukopenia also increased the risk of H7N9 influenza.
Suspect avian influenza in patients with febrile influenza-like illness and possible exposure to poultry or humans infected with H5N1 virus.
RT-PCR on nasal aspirate is the most reliable test.

First-line treatment is oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days based on several small uncontrolled trials (oseltamivir 150 mg twice daily for 10 days is an option if progression to pneumonia presents at onset). B
Optionally, adding baloxavir 40 to 80 mg once may reduce shedding but has not been shown to reduce mortality or length of hospital stay in a study of severe influenza. B
Based on its efficacy in influenza A and B, chemoprophylaxis is recommended for household contacts (oseltamivir 75 mg/day for 7-10 days after last known exposure). C

World Health Organization advance guideline recommends first-line treatment with oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days in patients age 13 years and older. Weight- and age-adjusted dosing is recommended for children ages 1 to 12. Recommendations are based on small uncontrolled trials observing increased survival among patients treated compared with untreated patients, and shorter time from onset to treatment in survivors than in nonsurvivors.
Based on high replication rates in vitro, consider oseltamivir 150 mg twice daily for 10 days, especially in patients with pneumonia or worsening condition.

Second-line therapy, based on extension from severe seasonal influenza, is adding baloxavir 40 mg to 80 mg to oseltamivir. This was shown in an RCT of 366 patients hospitalized with severe influenza to reduce shedding but not improve clinical outcomes.

Prophylaxis is recommended for close household contacts and other high-risk exposures, using oseltamivir 75 mg once daily (weight and age adjusted in younger children) for 7 to 10 days after the last known contact. Zanamivir 10 mg once daily is a second-line alternative for prophylaxis. Moderate-risk exposures (close contact with sick or dead animals, health care workers) should also consider prophylaxis.
There are insufficient data regarding combination therapy (e.g., with oseltamivir and rimantidine).
Consider corticosteroids in cases of septic shock with adrenal insufficiency.
For patients with suspected avian influenza, hospitalization is recommended with appropriate isolation.
ICU monitoring is often needed.
Natural history is pneumonia, followed by acute respiratory distress syndrome, multi-organ failure, and death (185 out of 304 reported cases as of 2008). B

However, in contrast to these earlier global outbreaks with high mortality, an overview of 46 recent U.S. cases associated with the dairy cattle outbreak have had no hospitalizations or deaths among those with known animal exposure, and there is currently no evidence of person-to-person transmission.
In four case series with 26 to 123 patients, the time between onset of illness to hospitalization was 3 to 5 days, and the time between onset of illness to death was 9 to 10 days. B
Monitor oxygen saturation and virological response, before and during treatment. C
Recommendations for treatment of confirmed or strongly suspected infection apply to pregnant women.
Chemoprophylaxis recommendations also apply to pregnant women at high or moderate risk.
Amantadine and rimantidine are not recommended for prophylaxis in pregnant women.
